name: Umar Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the fry and grill section at The Lobster Pot, a seafood restaurant right on the harbour in a little coastal town. In summer we do maybe two hundred and fifty covers a day, fish and chips, grilled mackerel, crab cakes, and I'm in from ten till close. I fillet the morning catch, make batter, and then it's fryers and the grill all evening. I like the fresh fish and the view from the back door, but winter is the hard part.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because the tourists go and the owner, Jim, cuts us to three days a week from November to March. I live on my own in a rented flat above the chandlery, so there's nobody to split the bills with. I've got about a hundred and fifty pounds saved right now, which is nothing. In winter there are maybe two other kitchens open in town, and they've got their own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, like most things, and leave it at that. At work I'd say the fish still needs filleting and the batter still needs mixing. Online I might share a joke about it, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it changes nothing, and that's the problem. My problem is winter, and AI was never going to fix three-day weeks. Every January I'm using the overdraft by the second week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at The Lobster Pot, because there's nothing better nearby. I'd look for winter work again, last year I did shifts at the fish processing plant, which was cold but paid. And I'd try to save more in August, when the tips are good, instead of spending them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels the same as every autumn, a bit of dread about the winter coming. Not panic, just that familiar knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you lose in winter, in real money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five hundred a month for five months, so two and a half thousand a year. That's more than I've ever had in the bank at once. The overdraft takes the hit and I spend summer paying it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the fish plant work involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Packing and grading fish on a line, early shifts, in a room just above freezing. It's honest work but they've already put a machine in that grades by camera. So I'm not sure they'll want me this winter.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, like most things.
I'd say the fish still needs **filleting** and the batter still needs mixing.
think: I think my real problem is **winter three-day weeks**, which AI never fixes.
I think I'm in my **overdraft** by the second week of every January.
do: Keep cooking at **The Lobster Pot** through the season.
Look for **winter shifts** at the fish processing plant.
Save **August tips** instead of spending them.
feel: He feels the **familiar knot** of dread before winter comes.
S0.quote: My problem is winter, and AI was never going to fix three-day weeks.
fieldNote: Umar's **seasonal hours** cost him about two and a half thousand a year.
He notices the fish plant's **camera grading** machine even in a plateau world.
He lives **alone**, so has no one to share bills with.

steps.text: Keep the fry and grill job at The Lobster Pot
Apply for winter packing shifts at the fish plant
Put August tips straight into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for the paperwork side, but kitchens are kitchens. At work I'd tell Jim to use it for bookings, because he spends hours on the phone. Online I'd keep quiet, I don't like arguing with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it'd make Jim's life easier, and maybe that's good for me. If bookings and ordering are quicker, he might keep the place open a bit longer in winter. But the fish plant was my winter backup, and the fish plant work goes to machines faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the AI booking tool with Jim once I'd seen another restaurant use it properly. I'd look for a new winter backup, maybe the care home kitchen up the hill. And I'd ask Jim about opening Friday and Saturday nights in winter with a smaller menu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mixed. A bit hopeful for the restaurant, a bit worried about my winter money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said once you'd seen another restaurant use it. Who would you look to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Anchor across the harbour, they're bigger and they try things first. If their bookings went well, I'd tell Jim. I'm not going to be the guinea pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a winter weekend opening mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two more days' pay, so maybe two hundred a month extra in winter. It would mean less overdraft and less stress in January. Jim's not against it, he just can't face the admin.

say: I'd say AI makes sense for **paperwork**, but kitchens stay kitchens.
I'd tell Jim to use it for **bookings** instead of the phone.
think: I think easier admin might keep the restaurant **open in winter**.
I think my **fish plant** backup goes to machines faster.
do: Try the **AI booking tool** once The Anchor proves it works.
Apply to the **care home kitchen** as winter backup.
feel: He feels **mixed**, hopeful for the restaurant but worried about winter money.
S1.quote: The fish plant was my winter backup, and the fish plant work goes to machines faster.
fieldNote: Umar sees AI admin as possibly **extending winter hours**.
He waits for **proof** from a rival restaurant before trying anything.
Losing the **fish plant** backup is his main new risk.

steps.text: Set up AI bookings after The Anchor proves it works
Apply to the care home kitchen for winter shifts
Pitch weekend winter openings with a short menu to Jim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and the government needs to do something now. At work I'd say we should all stick together and see what Jim plans. I'd tell my brother it's time to make some hard choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in trouble. By 2028 the AI runs the bookings and buying, and by 2031 a robot can fillet and fry. I'm a hands-on cook with no savings, living alone, in a seasonal town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get something steadier, maybe the hospital kitchen in the city, which means moving. I'd look at training as a boat mechanic, because the harbour always needs those and robots on boats seem further off. And I'd ask my brother if I could stay with him for a few months to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the tide going out fast and leaving me on the mud. I'd be scared, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots on boats seem further off. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Boats are cramped, wet and every one is different, like old houses. I've watched the mechanics down there, it's all bent arms and odd bolts. But I'm guessing, I don't actually know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years where Jim still needs my hands but the computer does his thinking. I'd use them to train and save, and I'd work every hour he offers. The worst thing would be to waste them hoping it's not real.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and government must act now.
I'd say staff should **stick together** and hear Jim's plans.
think: I think I'm **in trouble**, with robots filleting and frying by 2031.
I think living **alone** with no savings in a seasonal town is risky.
do: Look for a **hospital kitchen** job in the city.
Train as a **boat mechanic** for harbour work.
Stay with his **brother** for a few months to save.
feel: He feels **scared**, like the tide going out and leaving him on mud.
S2.quote: I'm a hands-on cook with no savings, living alone, in a seasonal town.
fieldNote: Umar picks **boat mechanics** because each job is different and cramped.
He admits he's **guessing** about which work robots reach later.
His brother is his only real **safety net**.

steps.text: Apply for hospital kitchen jobs in the city
Start an evening course in marine engine repair
Stay at his brother's place for a few months to save

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast but it's enough to get ready, if we start. At work I'd ask Jim straight what he'd do with the kitchen. I'd say the council should help seasonal towns, because we're always last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still worrying but it's different. Thinking AI by 2031 and robots around 2034 is about eight years of cooking. That's enough time to do a marine course part time and get my savings up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time marine engine course in the winter, when I've got the free days anyway. I'd save harder in summer, maybe a thousand by the end of the first season. And I'd use AI on my phone to help me study, since my brother says it explains things well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels tense but workable. The winters would be busy for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Using winter downtime for training. Is that realistic with money so tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the course is free or cheap, yes, because I'm home anyway. If the marine course is expensive, I'd be picking between the course and the heating. So it depends on the council, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Sami, he's an electrician and he did his training late. He'd tell me to stop talking and sign up. He'd be right, too.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ready** if we start now.
I'd say the council should help **seasonal towns** first.
think: I think I have about **eight years** of cooking left.
I think there's time for a **marine course** and better savings.
do: Start a **marine engine course** part time in winter.
Save **a thousand** by the end of the first summer.
Use **AI on his phone** to help him study.
feel: He feels **tense but workable**, with busy winters for once.
S3.quote: If the marine course is expensive, I'd be picking between the course and the heating.
fieldNote: Umar turns **winter downtime** into study time.
His plan depends on **cheap courses** from the council.

steps.text: Start a part-time marine engine course this winter
Save a thousand pounds from summer tips and wages
Use an AI study helper for the engine course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, so let's be sensible and plan. At work I'd say it's not something to lose sleep over yet. I'd tell people to learn a second trade if they can, because I think that's just good sense anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2039 means I'd cook until I'm about forty. That's fine, but it doesn't fix the winters. I'd still be on three days a week every November, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at The Lobster Pot and keep looking for steady winter work. I'd take the marine course slowly over a few years. And I'd try to use AI for the restaurant's bookings with Jim, once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels a lot easier on the AI side. The money side stays as it's always been, which is worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to winter. If winter were fixed, how would you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably calm, to be honest. If I had year-round full hours, I'd be fine for years. The robots don't worry me, the empty dining room in February does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the coast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it every January. But my brother is here, and I'd miss the harbour. If I had to choose between the sea and a steady wage, I honestly don't know.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long way off**, so plan sensibly.
I'd tell people to learn a **second trade** anyway.
think: I think I can cook until about **forty** before robots arrive.
I think the **winters** stay hard, AI or not.
do: Keep cooking at **The Lobster Pot** and seek winter work.
Take the **marine course** slowly over a few years.
Try **AI bookings** with Jim once proven.
feel: He feels **easier about AI**, but still worried about winter money.
S4.quote: The robots don't worry me, the empty dining room in February does.
fieldNote: Umar's mood is driven by **seasonal pay**, not the AGI date.
He'd feel **calm** if he had full hours all year.

steps.text: Keep the fry and grill job and look for winter work
Take one marine engine module each winter
Help Jim set up AI bookings once proven elsewhere

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no savings, no second trade and nobody to share the rent. What would help is a free course I could do in winter, and some kind of support for seasonal workers so the bad months aren't so bad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the season, and in a harbour town that's everything. Everybody here lives by the tourists. Robots or not, in a harbour town, if the tourists stay home, we all sink.

headlineQuote: In a harbour town, if the tourists stay home, we all sink.
portrait: Umar is a 27-year-old **fry and grill cook** at a harbour seafood restaurant.
He lives **alone** above a chandlery and has about a hundred and fifty saved.
His hours drop to **three days** a week every winter.
He waits for **proof** before trying new tech, then uses it.
He sees **marine engine** work as a possible second trade.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, with no savings or second trade.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a free **winter course** and support for **seasonal workers**.
